forces: Orchestra; arrangement attributed to Karl Müller-Berghaus
intro: Stokowski and the Philadelphia Orchestra play Liszt’s Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2 in C♯ minor, S. 244/2, in Karl Müller-Berghaus’s orchestral arrangement. This is the opening disc side of their 1936 recording.

sections.mNote: Stronger orchestral phrases return before the side ends.

cues.title: Lassan, introduction
cues.text: The Lassan, the slow first half of Liszt’s rhapsody, opens with a brief introduction and then moves into its minor key. Grave phrases alternate with lighter ones. In this arrangement the orchestra plays the contrasting sections of the piano original.
cues.evidence: The Lassan’s introduction and contrasting character are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2. The recording source attributes the arrangement to Müller-Berghaus: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:PDP-CH_-_Philadelphia_Orchestra_-_Stokowski_-_Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2_in_C-sharp_minor,_S_244-2_-_Liszt_-_Hmv-db3086-2a03100.flac.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Keys of the three versions
cues.text: The piano original is in C♯ minor. Liszt’s orchestral version, made with Franz Doppler, is in D minor; Müller-Berghaus takes it down to C minor.
cues.evidence: Leslie Howard distinguishes the piano original, Liszt–Doppler orchestration in D minor and Müller-Berghaus arrangement in C minor: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA67418%2F9. The selected recording’s attribution comes from its Commons description.

cues.title: Stokowski without a baton, 1929–30
cues.text: Late in the 1929–30 season Stokowski began conducting without a baton. In Philadelphia he experimented with seating, bowing and the lighting. At one concert the hall was darkened and only his head and hands were lit.
cues.evidence: Stokowski’s free-hand conducting, orchestral experiments and concert lighting are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopold_Stokowski, under Philadelphia Orchestra. The lighting episode is biographical, separate from this recording session.

composer.born: 22 October 1811, Doborján, Kingdom of Hungary (now Raiding, Austria)
composer.epithet: Pianist whose playing drew orchestral sound from the keyboard, and who at the end of his life turned to sparse music at the piano.
facts: Carl Czerny and Antonio Salieri in Vienna; Anton Reicha in Paris
Free masterclasses; founding president of the Budapest music academy, 1875
Piano works and transcriptions; thirteen symphonic poems; symphonies, concertos and sacred music
composer.background:
Writing from Albano in June 1839, Liszt told Princess Cristina Belgiojoso about the concerts he had been giving alone in Rome. No singer came on between his pieces, and no other soloist shared the bill. He played his transcription of the William Tell Overture, fantasies on opera tunes, studies and improvisations. Between numbers he talked to the audience. “The concert is me,” he joked.

His father Adam had begun the piano lessons in Doborján, a German-speaking village in the Kingdom of Hungary, where he worked on an Esterházy estate. Liszt always counted Hungary as his homeland, though the languages he used most easily were German and French. The family went to Vienna in 1822. Carl Czerny, a former pupil of Beethoven, taught him piano, and Antonio Salieri taught him composition. In 1823 the family moved to Paris, where the Conservatoire refused to admit a foreigner. He continued his education with private lessons, including work with Anton Reicha.
